source: AACE, Delayed Hospital Handovers: Impact Assessment of Patient Harm (November 2021), summarised on the AACE Hospital Handovers webpage (accessed 2026)
wording: Over eight in ten of those whose 'handover' (from ambulance clinician to hospital clinician) was delayed beyond 60 minutes were assessed as having potentially experienced some level of harm; 53% low harm, 23% moderate harm and 9% (one patient in ten) could have been said to have experienced severe harm.

source: AACE, Hospital Handovers (webpage, accessed 2026)
wording: The nationally defined target for hospitals included in the NHS Standard Contract states that all handovers between ambulance and A&E must take place within 15 minutes, with none waiting more than 30 minutes.

source: APAGBI/ESPA/ADARPEF Consensus statement on clear fluids fasting for elective paediatric general anaesthesia (Thomas et al., Pediatric Anesthesia 2018)
wording: based on the current evidence base, unless there is a clear contraindication, it is safe and recommended for all children able to take clear fluids, to be allowed and encouraged to have them up to 1 hour before elective general anesthesia.

source: APAGBI/ESPA/ADARPEF Consensus statement on clear fluids fasting for elective paediatric general anaesthesia (Thomas et al., Pediatric Anesthesia 2018), Table 1
wording: Preoperative fasting for elective procedures in children, Age (y) 0-16: Solid food, Formula milk 6h; Breast milk 4h; Clear fluids 1h.

source: ARSAC Notes for Guidance on the Clinical Administration of Radiopharmaceuticals and Use of Sealed Radioactive Sources (January 2016), Section 7, paragraph 7.8
wording: Specific instructions must be given to the mother of an infant in order to minimise irradiation to the latter.

source: ARSAC Notes for Guidance on the Clinical Administration of Radiopharmaceuticals and Use of Sealed Radioactive Sources (January 2016), paragraph 3.12
wording: Where two imaging investigations exist that give equivalent information and both are available to the patient within the timeframe of their clinical management, then on radiation protection grounds the investigation not utilising ionising radiation should be used.

source: ARSAC Notes for Guidance on the Clinical Administration of Radiopharmaceuticals and Use of Sealed Radioactive Sources (January 2016), paragraphs 7.11-7.12 and Table 7.1
wording: In some circumstances it will be necessary to advise females not to become pregnant for a period following the administration of long-lived radiopharmaceuticals. The female patient should be advised to avoid pregnancy for a period following therapy administration as given in Table 7.1.

source: ARSAC Notes for Guidance on the Clinical Administration of Radiopharmaceuticals and Use of Sealed Radioactive Sources (January 2016), paragraphs 7.4-7.5
wording: Where a patient is probably or definitely pregnant, the justification for the procedure should be considered by the ARSAC certificate holder following consultation with the clinician responsible for the patient... The principle adopted here is that the absorbed dose to a foetus should not exceed 1 mGy.

source: Academy of Medical Royal Colleges and RCR, Alerts and notification of imaging reports: recommendations (October 2022), recommendation on critical imaging alerts 7
wording: 7. Referrers must ensure a valid contact detail is available, including out of hours, on all imaging referrals. They must also ensure that all reports are read, acknowledged and acted upon (or plan to act).

source: Academy of Medical Royal Colleges and RCR, Alerts and notification of imaging reports: recommendations (October 2022), recommendations on cancer imaging alerts 1 and 2
wording: 1. All imaging reports with expected or unexpected new cancer diagnosis or newly detected cancer recurrence should be notified to the referrers with a CANCER alert in the report via a digital platform immediately upon completion of the reports. 2. Referring teams must ensure a valid contact detail (or through a pre-agreed system) is available, including out of hours, on all imaging referrals. They must also ensure that all reports are read, acknowledged and acted upon (or plan to act).

source: Academy of Medical Royal Colleges and RCR, Alerts and notification of imaging reports: recommendations (October 2022), recommendations on critical imaging alerts 2 and 4
wording: 2. If immediate intervention is required, the alert should be supplemented by direct verbal communication. 4. The verbal communication including the name of the person who receives the results should be documented in the imaging report or patient record.

source: Academy of Medical Royal Colleges, Please write to me: guidance for writing directly to patients (April 2026 update), 'Making your writing easier to read and understand'
wording: Avoid complex words and sentences. Measure the Flesch reading ease score and the UK reading age using the NHS Medical Document Readability Tool. Aim for a Flesch reading ease score of 70 or above and a UK reading age of 9–11 years.

source: Academy of Medical Royal Colleges, Please write to me: guidance for writing directly to patients (April 2026 update), 'Structure and content of outpatient letters'
wording: An outpatient clinic letter should include: ... A hospital phone number and email address for follow-up questions and correcting errors.

source: Academy of Medical Royal Colleges, Please write to me: guidance for writing directly to patients (April 2026 update), section 'Electronic Patient Records and Artificial Intelligence'
wording: Templates for creating letters within the Electronic Patient Record (EPR) should be consistent with the sections listed above. The default format should be a letter addressed to the patient.

source: AoMRC Evidence-Based Interventions: knee MRI when symptoms are suggestive of osteoarthritis (2020, reviewed 2024)
wording: An initial diagnosis of OA can be made when clinical assessment is suggestive of this pathology. If imaging is required to confirm the diagnosis, then weight bearing radiographs are the first-line of investigation. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for knees is not usually needed.

source: AoMRC Evidence-Based Interventions: knee arthroscopy for patients with osteoarthritis (2019, reviewed 2024); NICE NG226 rec 1.7.1 (2022)
wording: Referral for arthroscopic lavage and debridement should not be offered as part of treatment for osteoarthritis, unless the person has knee osteoarthritis with a clear history of mechanical locking. (EBI). NICE NG226 1.7.1: Do not offer arthroscopic lavage or debridement to people with osteoarthritis.

source: AoMRC Evidence-Based Interventions: scans for shoulder pain and guided injections (2020, reviewed 2024)
wording: Image guided subacromial injections are not recommended in primary, intermediate or secondary care. Evidence does not support the use of guided subacromial injections over unguided subacromial injections in the treatment of subacromial shoulder pain.

source: Association of Anaesthetists and British and Irish Hypertension Society, Measurement and management of adult blood pressure in the peri-operative period (Anaesthesia 2026)
wording: A blood pressure measurement should be performed in the pre-operative clinic using best practice as outlined in this guideline. Surgery should proceed unless the blood pressure is ≥ 180/120 (stage 3 hypertension).

source: Association of Anaesthetists and British and Irish Hypertension Society, Measurement and management of adult blood pressure in the peri-operative period (Anaesthesia 2026), recommendation 6
wording: Patients at risk of postural hypotension including those who are symptomatic, aged > 80 y or who are diabetic, should be screened with a supine-to-stand blood pressure assessment or a sit-to-stand assessment (if more pragmatic).

source: Association of Anaesthetists and British and Irish Hypertension Society, Measurement and management of adult blood pressure in the peri-operative period (Anaesthesia 2026), recommendation 7
wording: Patients should normally take their antihypertensive therapy, including angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers, on the day of surgery (moderate recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence).

source: Association of Anaesthetists and Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, Peri-operative management of diabetes mellitus: consensus statement (Anaesthesia 2026)
wording: Check a capillary blood glucose every hour for patients who are placed on a variable rate intravenous insulin infusion.

source: Association of Anaesthetists guidelines: safe vascular access 2025 (Anaesthesia 2025)
wording: All possible procedures should be put in place to prevent retained guidewires, including operator vigilance; guidewire counts; mandatory witnessed documentation of guidewire removal; and where available, the use of guidewire anti-retention devices.

source: Association of Anaesthetists guidelines: the use of blood components and their alternatives (Anaesthesia 2025), recommendation 2
wording: Where blood transfusion is anticipated, this and alternatives to transfusion should be discussed with the patient before surgery, and their consent should be documented according to local protocols.

source: Association of Anaesthetists of Great Britain and Ireland recommended fasting times, cited in the PIER Network Peri-operative Fasting Policy (October 2020)
wording: The Association of Anaesthetists Great Britain and Ireland (AAGBI) states that recommended fasting times are six hours for food, four hours for breast milk and two hours for clear fluids.

source: Association of Anaesthetists, CPOC, RCoA and partners, Elective peri-operative management of adults taking GLP-1 RAs, GIP/GLP-1 RAs and SGLT2 inhibitors: consensus statement (Anaesthesia 2025)
wording: Individualised pulmonary aspiration risk assessment should be completed, accounting for drug, patient and procedural factors.

source: Association of Anaesthetists, RCP and Society for Endocrinology UK. Guidelines for the management of glucocorticoids during the peri-operative period for patients with adrenal insufficiency (Anaesthesia 2020), recommendation 1 and Table 2
wording: Prescribed glucocorticoid therapy (prednisolone ≥ 5 mg per day in adults or hydrocortisone-equivalent dose of 10–15 mg.m−2 per day in children) across all routes of administration (oral, inhaled, topical, intranasal, intra-articular), can cause suppression of the hypothalamo–pituitary–adrenal axis, and is the most common cause of adrenal insufficiency that anaesthetists will encounter. ... Table 2 Recommended doses for intra- and postoperative steroid cover in adults receiving adrenosuppresive doses of steroids (prednisolone equivalent ≥ 5 mg for 4 weeks or longer). Major surgery: Hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenously at induction, followed by immediate initiation of a continuous infusion of hydrocortisone at 200 mg.24 h−1; Alternatively, dexamethasone 6–8 mg intravenously, if used, will suffice for 24 h

source: BAETS Consensus, Pre and Post Operative Laryngoscopy in Thyroid and Parathyroid Surgery (FF Palazzo for BAETS, June 2010)
wording: Post-operative laryngoscopy is required as a key quality control measure and should become mandatory.

source: BAETS Post-operative Hypocalcaemia Guidance
wording: POST THYROIDECTOMY / PARATHYROIDECTOMY CORRECTED CALCIUM LEVELS: Check within 12h postoperatively

source: BAPEN MUST (Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool)
wording: Refer to dietitian, Nutritional Support Team or implement local policy. Set goals, improve and increase overall nutritional intake. Monitor and review care plan.

source: BAPM Framework for Practice: Identification and Management of Neonatal Hypoglycaemia in the Full Term Infant, Practice Point 15 (2024)
wording: Measure the BG level before the second feed (2 to 4 hours after birth). If the baby shows feeding cues before 2 hours do not restrict feeding and allow baby to feed. Measure BG immediately if there are clinical signs suggestive of hypoglycaemia (Practice Point 2).

source: BASHH UK guideline for the use of HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (2021, amended 2023), auditable outcome measure 3
wording: Proportion of PEP prescriptions that fit within recommended indications (consider or recommended): aim 90%

source: BASHH UK national guideline for the management of infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae (2025), auditable outcome measures
wording: All individuals with gonorrhoea should have cultures taken for susceptibility testing prior to treatment (performance standard 97%).

source: BASHH UK national guideline for the use of doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis (2025), auditable outcome measures
wording: All people prescribed doxyPEP should be assessed for eligibility for HIV PrEP (performance standard 97%)

source: BASHH UK national guidelines on the management of syphilis (2024), auditable outcomes
wording: The percentage of confirmed syphilis cases having a record of an RPR titre obtained 6 months post-treatment (standard 65% confirmed syphilis cases).

source: BASK Arthroscopic Meniscal Surgery: A National Society Treatment Guideline and Consensus Statement (Bone Joint J 2019;101-B:652-659)
wording: It was agreed that for the guidance from the flowchart to be applicable, MRI confirmation of a lesion would be necessary.

source: BASK Arthroscopic Meniscal Surgery: A National Society Treatment Guideline and Consensus Statement (Bone Joint J 2019;101-B:652-659), Meniscal Tear Management Guideline flowchart
wording: Locked Knee: Assessment: Arthroscopic meniscal surgery indicated. Recommendation: Urgent Arthroscopic Meniscal Surgery.

source: BESS Patient Care Pathway: Subacromial Pain (Shoulder & Elbow 2025;17(6)); AoMRC EBI arthroscopic shoulder decompression (reviewed 2024)
wording: Physiotherapy or non-surgical treatment should be first line of management. If symptoms fail to resolve with non-surgical treatment by six months, then there is moderate evidence that surgical treatment could be considered and subacromial decompression may offer satisfactory long-term outcomes for patients with subacromial pain. In addition, patients should be made aware that there are studies which show no evidence of the benefit of surgery compared to sham surgery.

source: BESS patient care pathway: Tennis elbow (Shoulder & Elbow 2023;15(4):348-359), Outcome metrics section
wording: The core outcome set for LET defined by Bateman et al. PRTEE; PRTEE pain & function subscale.

source: BESS patient care pathway: Tennis elbow (Shoulder & Elbow 2023;15(4):348-359), Primary care/community triage services section
wording: Plain radiographs of the elbow are not essential for confirming the diagnosis. Specialist imaging such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or computed tomography (CT) scans are not needed for treatment of LET in the primary care setting.

source: BESS patient care pathway: Tennis elbow (Shoulder & Elbow 2023;15(4):348-359), summary of recommendations
wording: Corticosteroid injection should not be used in the treatment of LET [lateral elbow tendinopathy] - Strong recommendation.

source: BESS/BOA Patient Care Pathway: Glenohumeral osteoarthritis (Shoulder & Elbow 2016;8(3))
wording: Acceptable scores include the Disability of Arm, Shoulder and Hand, Constant Score and the Oxford Shoulder Score. Other measures such as EQ5D may be used for economic analysis. Scores should be captured pre-operatively and a minimum of 6 months following intervention, which allows longitudinal analysis to determine magnitude of treatment effect and consequences of any treatment-related adverse events.

source: BESS/BOA Patient Care Pathway: Traumatic anterior shoulder instability (Shoulder & Elbow 2015;7(3):214-226)
wording: Patients between the ages of 40 years and 60 years have an increased risk of clinically relevant rotator cuff tears (approximately 40%) and, consequently should undergo routine ultrasound/magnetic resonance imaging to assess cuff integrity.

source: BMA, Resuscitation Council UK and RCN, Decisions relating to cardiopulmonary resuscitation, 3rd edition (1st revision) 2016, section 15
wording: Good documentation includes the following, on the CPR decision form or in the main health record or in some cases both: … details of any discussions about the decision with the patient, with those close to them, and (for a person who does not have capacity) with any person with authority to make decisions on their behalf and/ or with an IMCA • where no discussions have taken place the reasons for this

source: BOA Specialty Standard: Best Practice for Management of Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Injuries (September 2020), standard 10
wording: Decision to return to sport should be criteria based taking into consideration physical factors relating to the knee; psychological factors including fear of reinjury and social factors; while being tailored to the specific sport. To assess readiness to return to play and the risk for reinjury, a range of tests, including strength tests, hop tests and measurement of movement quality, should be used.

source: BOA Specialty Standard: Best Practice for Management of Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Injuries (September 2020), standard 3
wording: All patients being considered for surgery should be offered prehabilitation to recover knee movement and quadriceps strength.

source: BOA Specialty Standard: Best Practice for Management of Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Injuries (September 2020), standard 7b
wording: Graft selection should be discussed including autograft, allograft and synthetic ligaments. This should include the benefits, complications and risks of all and the preferred graft recommendation.

source: BOA Specialty Standard: Best Practice for Management of Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Injuries (September 2020), standard 7d
wording: Consent for inclusion into National Ligament Registry should be sought and patients should be registered in its database. Hospitals should facilitate the accurate recording of surgical procedures and patients' outcome by providing appropriate clerical and IT support.

source: BOA Specialty Standard: Best Practice for Management of Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Injuries (September 2020), standard 8a
wording: The procedure should be performed on a Day Case basis, for majority of patients. The surgery should be performed by or under supervision of a surgeon with special interest in soft tissue knee reconstruction.

source: BOA Specialty Standard: Best Practice for Management of Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Injuries (September 2020), standard 8d
wording: An examination under anaesthetic must be performed to take into account the degree of anteroposterior and rotational laxity as well as any other associated injuries and documented.

source: BOA Specialty Standard: Investigation and Management of Patients with Problematic Knee Replacements (August 2020), standard 2
wording: Initial investigation should include: clinical examination, X-Ray imaging and serological screening tests for infection (e.g. CRP, ESR +/- PV).

source: BOA Specialty Standard: Investigation and Management of Patients with Problematic Knee Replacements (August 2020), standard 4
wording: Full weight bearing AP and lateral, long-leg alignment and patella skyline radiographs should be performed in all patients.

source: BOA Specialty Standard: Investigation and Management of Prosthetic Joint Infection in Knee Replacement (August 2020), standard 12
wording: Antibiotics should not be administered for 2 weeks prior to aspiration +/- biopsy except in cases of acute infection in a systemically unwell (septic) patient.

source: BOA Specialty Standard: The Assessment of Patients with Recurrent Patellar Instability (August 2020), standard 2
wording: Radiographs should include: antero-posterior (or PA); true lateral at 20-30 degrees flexion; and axial (skyline) views at 20-30 degrees knee flexion.

source: BOA Specialty Standard: The Assessment of Patients with Recurrent Patellar Instability (August 2020), standards 3 and 5
wording: Further imaging investigations should include an MRI of the knee (unless MRI contra-indicated) which includes axial and sagittal images. The MRI aims to outline: Patella alta ...; Degenerative change or cartilage loss; Loose osteochondral or chondral fragment; Meniscal and ligamentous pathology; Trochlear dysplasia; Tibial tuberosity offset. ... Determination of patella alta involves assessment of the clinical picture and radiological imaging, and may include indices such as patellotrochlear overlap, Caton-Dechamps ratio or Blackburne-Peel ratio according to published normal ranges.

source: BOA Standard: Assessment and Management of First Time Lateral Patellar Dislocation (FTLPD) (December 2024), standard 13
wording: Clinicians considering surgery following FTLPD should discuss their plan within an age-appropriate multi-disciplinary team meeting, or alternative forum for peer review, with written documentation of the outcome included in the medical records.

source: BOA Standard: Assessment and Management of First Time Lateral Patellar Dislocation (FTLPD) (December 2024), standard 15
wording: Appropriate patient information including leaflets, videos or online / app-based content should be available.

source: BOA Standard: Assessment and Management of First Time Lateral Patellar Dislocation (FTLPD) (December 2024), standard 8
wording: Assessment by a musculo-skeletal physiotherapist should occur within 3 weeks of injury.

source: BOA/BAPRAS Audit Standards for Trauma: Open Fractures (December 2017), standard 14
wording: Definitive soft tissue closure or coverage should be achieved within 72 hours of injury if it cannot be performed at the time of debridement.

source: BOA/BAPRAS Audit Standards for Trauma: Open Fractures (December 2017), standard 2
wording: Intravenous prophylactic antibiotics should be administered as soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour of injury.

source: BOA/BAPRAS Audit Standards for Trauma: Open Fractures (December 2017), standards 9 and 10
wording: Photographs of open fracture wounds should be taken when they are first exposed for clinical care, before debridement and at other key stages of management. These should be kept in the patient's records.

source: BOA/BAPRAS/Vascular Society Standard: Diagnosis and management of arterial injuries associated with musculoskeletal trauma (June 2026), standard 10
wording: Revascularisation is an emergency procedure (NCEPOD 1) and should be commenced within one hour of arrival to hospital.

source: BOA/BAPRAS/Vascular Society Standard: Diagnosis and management of arterial injuries associated with musculoskeletal trauma (June 2026), standard 8
wording: CT angiogram is recommended if arterial injury is suspected and should be performed concurrently with whole-body CT.

source: BOAST Acute Management of Peri-Prosthetic Joint Infection (BOA, October 2023, updated April 2024), standard 1
wording: Guidance on who to contact and how to respond to a patient with suspected PJI should be readily available to Primary Care providers and Emergency department practitioners, and be included in discharge documentation.

source: BOAST Acute Management of Peri-Prosthetic Joint Infection (BOA, October 2023, updated April 2024), standard 4
wording: A patient who is not septic should not be given antibiotics until appropriate deep tissue samples have been taken.

source: BOAST Acute Management of Peri-Prosthetic Joint Infection (October 2023), standard 3.3
wording: requires emergent drainage and should have surgery performed by a suitably experienced surgical team as soon as is safe. In an acutely unwell patient this should be within 6 hours unless there are specific reasons that this is not possible.

source: BOAST Acute Management of Peri-Prosthetic Joint Infection (October 2023), standard 5.2
wording: a general assessment for additional sources of infection including a cardiovascular assessment for endocarditis.

source: BOAST Acute Management of Peri-Prosthetic Joint Infection (October 2023), standard 6
wording: Initial investigations should include Full Blood Count, CRP, renal function, and plain radiographs.

source: BOAST Assessment and Management of First Time Lateral Patellar Dislocation (December 2024)
wording: Following reduction, all patients should have an AP and lateral radiograph of the knee, including skyline patellar view.

source: BOAST Assessment of the Spine in the Trauma Patient (April 2025)
wording: Fracture, subluxation or ligamentous injury of the cervical spine requires CT angiography to exclude blunt cerebrovascular injury (Denver criteria)

source: BOAST Diagnosis and Management of Compartment Syndrome of the Extremities (updated July 2025)
wording: Patients at risk of ACS should be assessed hourly with documentation of findings (whether present or not), an interpretation of these findings and rationale for management.

source: BOAST Early Management of the Paediatric Forearm Fracture (May 2021), standard 11
wording: Oral analgesia to take home and dedicated information leaflets, that include red flag symptoms and contact details, should be provided. Prior to discharge, a fracture clinic appointment should be made to occur within 7 days of injury.

source: BOAST Early Management of the Paediatric Forearm Fracture (May 2021), standard 12
wording: A documented review of the case and images by a consultant orthopaedic surgeon should occur within 48 hours of injury.

source: BOAST Early Management of the Paediatric Forearm Fracture (May 2021), standards 2 and 9
wording: A documented assessment of the limb, performed on presentation, should include the status of the radial pulse, digital capillary refill time and the individual function of the radial, median and ulnar nerves. ... Before discharge a recorded assessment of the neurovascular status of the limb should be repeated as described in standard two.

source: BOAST Fracture Related Infections (BOA, September 2019; still the current BOAST), 'Assessment of FRI' and 'Secondary fracture surgery'
wording: When debridement is indicated 5 samples should be taken from around the fracture site for microbiological culture using separate sterile instruments and a no touch technique for each. In all chronic infections and when the diagnosis is in doubt in acute infections take 2 samples for histology.

source: BOAST Fracture Related Infections (September 2019)
wording: A patient who is not systemically unwell should be reviewed by a consultant in a clinic within 48 hours. Antibiotic treatment should not be commenced before that review.

source: BOAST Fracture Related Infections (September 2019), standard 4E
wording: For stable patients the optimum antibiotic free duration before sampling should be discussed with microbiology. In non-acute infections this should be a minimum of 2 weeks.

source: BOAST Fracture Related Infections (September 2019), standard 5A
wording: Empiric antibiotics without a diagnostic work up should not be given and if already commenced should be stopped.

source: BOAST Fracture Related Infections (September 2019), standard 6
wording: The presence of infection should be considered in any patient having further surgery following initial fracture fixation for instance for non or delayed union. ... Where surgical exposure allows, 5 samples for microbiology (using separate sterile instruments) and 2 for histology should be taken at the time of subsequent surgery unless the fracture is soundly united with no evidence for infection and the procedure was for the elective removal of metalwork.

source: BOAST Fracture Related Infections (September 2019), standard 7B
wording: All in-patients with proven or suspected FRI should be the subject of weekly bone and joint infection MDT review to rationalise surgical strategy and antimicrobial management. MDT time should be sufficient to review relevant out-patients too.

source: BOAST Management of musculoskeletal soft tissue infections (July 2025)
wording: Native joint infections should be treated according to standards outlined in the BOASt for the acute management of periprosthetic joint infection2, recognising the time critical nature of chondral injury. Aspirate should include samples for crystallography.

source: BOAST Open Fractures (December 2017); NICE NG37 recs 1.3.5–1.3.6 (2016)
wording: Photographs of open fracture wounds should be taken when they are first exposed for clinical care, before debridement and at other key stages of management. These should be kept in the patient’s records.

source: BOAST Outpatient and on-call services for people with fractures or musculoskeletal injury (BOA, February 2026)
wording: A definitive treatment plan should be documented for all patients within 72 hours of first presentation and copied to the patient and their GP.

source: BOAST Outpatient and on-call services for people with fractures or musculoskeletal injury (BOA, February 2026); links to NICE NG89 rec 1.11.1 (2018)
wording: A documented risk assessment for venous thromboembolism (VTE) should be conducted for all patients with a lower limb injury. (NICE NG89)

source: BOAST Peripheral Nerve Injury (December 2021), standard 1.1.2
wording: 1. An examination to assess and document all the functions of a peripheral nerve: 1.1. should be carried out and recorded: ... 1.1.2. after any intervention to the limb such as injection, manipulation or application of cast

source: BOAST Peripheral Nerve Injury (December 2021), standard 1.1.4
wording: post-operatively, by the operating surgeon following any procedure where nerve injury is a recognised risk

source: BOAST Peripheral Nerve Injury (December 2021), standard 6.1
wording: 6. Formal advice should be sought: 6.1. Within twenty-four hours when a laceration or penetrating injury is associated with a neurological deficit.

source: BOAST Peripheral Nerve Injury (December 2021), standards 1.1.1–1.1.2
wording: 1. An examination to assess and document all the functions of a peripheral nerve: 1.1. should be carried out and recorded: 1.1.1. at the first opportunity after injury 1.1.2. after any intervention to the limb such as injection, manipulation or application of cast

source: BOAST Supracondylar Fractures of the Humerus in Children (October 2020), standard 12
wording: The operating surgeon should determine and document the need for post-operative radiographs and anticipated time of wire removal.

source: BOAST Supracondylar Fractures of the Humerus in Children (October 2020), standard 2
wording: Surgical management should be carried out on the day of injury. Night-time operating is not necessary unless there are indications for urgent surgery which should be documented.

source: BOAST Supracondylar Fractures of the Humerus in Children (October 2020), standard 6
wording: When a medial wire is used, techniques to avoid ulnar nerve injury should be employed and recorded on the operation note.

source: BOAST The Care of the Older or Frail Orthopaedic Trauma Patient (May 2019)
wording: Ceilings of treatment, including transfer, escalation and the appropriateness of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), should be discussed jointly by the treating teams. This should be documented and include the patient and those close to them, considering advanced directives, lasting powers of attorney and safeguarding issues. These decisions should be made at consultant level and prior to any surgery.

source: BOAST The Management of Ankle Fractures (August 2016)
wording: In fracture patterns where stability is uncertain, patients should be reviewed within 2 weeks with further radiographs (weight bearing if possible) to confirm the position remains acceptable.

source: BOAST The Management of Ankle Fractures (August 2016); NICE NG38 rec 1.4.2 (2016)
wording: Early fixation (on the day or day after injury) is recommended in the majority of patients under 60 years when the ankle mortise is unstable.

source: BOAST The Management of Ankle Fractures (BOA, August 2016), Standards for Practice
wording: Adequate reduction must be confirmed by review of repeat radiographs and documented before transfer from ED.

source: BOAST The Management of Children with Acute Musculoskeletal Infection (May 2022), standard 10
wording: Septic arthritis requires surgical drainage as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours of diagnosis.

source: BOAST The Management of Children with Acute Musculoskeletal Infection (May 2022), standard 14
wording: Bone and joint infection should be followed up clinically and radiographically for a minimum of 12 months by a clinician able to identify long-term complications.

source: BOAST The Management of Children with Acute Musculoskeletal Infection (May 2022), standard 6
wording: Essential haematological investigations include, in order, FBC, CRP, blood cultures*, ESR. Plain radiographs of the affected bone or joint are required. No single investigation algorithm is completely reliable: diagnosis should be considered in conjunction with history and examination.

source: BOAST The Management of Children with Acute Musculoskeletal Infection (May 2022), standard 7
wording: MRI is the preferred second line modality, ideally within 48 hours unless the clinical condition mandates more urgent imaging. Ultrasound should be performed within the same time frame.

source: BOAST The Management of Distal Radial Fractures (BOA, December 2017)
wording: Patients should be assessed for falls risks and bone health, and referred to the fracture liaison services and or falls service where appropriate.

source: BOAST The Management of Distal Radial Fractures (BOA, December 2017); also NICE NG38 rec 1.3.1 (2016)
wording: If manipulation is indicated, it should be undertaken using regional anaesthesia, performed by a suitably qualified and trained practitioner (as opposed to local haematoma block).

source: BOAST The Management of Distal Radial Fractures (December 2017)
wording: Repeat radiographs of the wrist between 1-2 weeks after injury (or manipulation) where it is thought that the fracture pattern is unstable AND when subsequent displacement will lead to surgical intervention.

source: BOAST The Management of Patients with Pelvic Fractures (January 2018)
wording: When there is a suspected active bleeding from a pelvic fracture, apply a pelvic binder in the correct position. This should be applied prehospital.

source: BOAST The Management of Urological Trauma Associated with Pelvic Fractures (August 2016)
wording: All patients suffering high-energy trauma must have examination of the perineum and genitalia plus a rectal examination and the findings recorded in the medical records.

source: BOASt Mobilisation and weightbearing after orthopaedic surgery or musculoskeletal injury (BOA, August 2024), standards 3–5; also BOASt Outpatient and on-call services for people with fractures or musculoskeletal injury (BOA, February 2026)
wording: 3. A weightbearing status should be attributed to each affected limb. 4. The following specific terms should be used to define weightbearing status: a. Non Weightbearing b. Limited Weightbearing c. Unrestricted Weightbearing 5. Terms such as touch, partial, proportional, permissive, or progressive weightbearing should no longer be used.

source: BOASt Outpatient and on-call services for people with fractures or musculoskeletal injury (BOA, February 2026), standard 2
wording: Patients must have their case reviewed by a named consultant within 24 hours of first presentation. This can be performed in person or virtually in a trauma meeting. The outcome of this review should be documented and a copy sent to the patient and GP.

source: BOASt Outpatient and on-call services for people with fractures or musculoskeletal injury (BOA, February 2026), standard 4
wording: A definitive treatment plan should be documented for all patients within 72 hours of first presentation and copied to the patient and their GP.

source: BOASt Outpatient and on-call services for people with fractures or musculoskeletal injury (BOA, February 2026), standard 7
wording: Information in an accessible format and language should be available and include instructions for casts, splints, slings, and appliances.

source: BSCOS Best Practice in Children's Trauma & Orthopaedics in the UK (November 2025), Section 3 Key Points: Life Changing Injuries
wording: Specific paediatric injuries that could have potentially life-changing results should be discussed at PRMs. These should include amongst others: open fractures, pelvic fractures, femoral neck fractures, Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis (SUFE), lower limb physeal fractures, intra-articular fractures and pathological fractures or fractures occurring in children with underlying musculoskeletal conditions

source: BSG/BASL guidelines on the management of ascites in cirrhosis, Gut 2021;70:9–29, recommendation 2.1
wording: Diagnostic paracentesis should be carried out without a delay to rule out spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) in all cirrhotic patients with ascites on hospital admission.

source: BSG/BASL guidelines on the management of ascites in cirrhosis, Gut 2021;70:9–29, recommendation 6.1
wording: Albumin (as 20% or 25% solution) should be infused after paracentesis of >5 L is completed at a dose of 8 g albumin/L of ascites removed.

source: BSSH Standards of Care in Hand Trauma: Flexor sheath infection (BSSH, 2021)
wording: Urgent – as early as possible within safe working hours and within a maximum of 24 hours of decision to operate

source: BSSH Standards of Care in Hand Trauma: Human and animal bites to the hand (BSSH, 2021)
wording: Antibiotics should be started as soon as possible after injury.

source: BSSH Standards of Care in Hand Trauma: Lacerations with flexor tendon involvement
wording: Referral category green – The patient should be seen at the next available soft tissue hand clinic (ideally within 24 hours).

source: BSSH Standards of Care in Hand Trauma: Mallet injuries (BSSH, published 2020)
wording: for closed injuries; green – next available clinic (real or virtual) within 72 hours

source: BSSH Standards of Care in Hand Trauma: Open fractures (BSSH, 2021)
wording: Antibiotics should be stopped at 72 hours or after definitive closure whichever is the sooner, subject to clinical judgement.

source: BSSH Standards of Care in Hand Trauma: Scaphoid fractures, standard 14 (BSSH, 2024; revision due 2027)
wording: Patients should only be discharged once union is confirmed on CT (>50% of the fracture cross-sectional area) or by delayed radiographs at 6 months.

source: BSSH Standards of Care in Hand Trauma: Scaphoid fractures, standard 8 (BSSH, 2024; revision due 2027)
wording: If a scaphoid fracture is visible on plain radiographs, CT scan should be performed to measure displacement accurately.

source: BTS Quality Standard for Pleural Disease, Quality statement 11 (2026)
wording: In the context of respiratory infective symptoms, a unilateral pleural effusion should be promptly recognised as potential pleural infection and sampled within 24 hours if appropriate to confirm or exclude the diagnosis.

source: BTS Quality Standard for Pleural Disease, Quality statement 16 (2026)
wording: Patients with spontaneous recurrent pneumothorax* should be considered for elective surgical recurrence prevention if clinically appropriate. *Recurrent pneumothorax includes patients with second ipsilateral or first contralateral pneumothorax.

source: BTS Quality Standard for Pleural Disease, Quality statement 3 (2026)
wording: Peri-procedural thoracic ultrasound must be used for all pleural fluid procedures unless real-time CT imaging is more appropriate.

source: BTS Quality Standard for Pleural Disease, quality statement on access to pleural services
wording: For symptomatic or undiagnosed pleural effusion, where a pleural procedure is clinically indicated, it should be offered within five days of the decision being made, unless the patient's symptoms or evidence of infection makes a more urgent procedure necessary.

source: BTS Quality Standards for acute NIV in adults, Quality statement 4 (2018)
wording: Patients who meet evidence-based criteria for acute NIV should start NIV within 60 min of the blood gas result associated with the clinical decision to provide NIV and within 120 min of hospital arrival for patients who present acutely.

source: BTS Quality Standards for acute NIV in adults, Quality statement 5 (2018)
wording: All patients should have a documented escalation plan before starting treatment with acute NIV.

source: BTS Quality Standards for acute NIV in adults, Quality statement 6 (2018)
wording: All patients treated with acute NIV should have blood gas analysis performed within 2 hours of starting acute NIV. Failure of these blood gas measurements to improve should trigger specialist healthcare professional review within 30 min.

source: BTS quality standards for the investigation and management of pulmonary nodules (BMJ Open Resp Res 2018), quality statement 4
wording: People with pulmonary nodules confirmed on CT are offered discharge, further surveillance, further workup or treatment according to BTS Guidelines

source: BTS/RCP/RCN emergency oxygen guideline, updated NICE NG115 COPD guideline, rec 1.2.9 (2018, updated 2019)
wording: Use a target oxygen saturation range of 88-92% for patients with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease who are at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, until blood gas results are available.

source: BTS/SIGN British guideline on the management of asthma (SIGN 158), section 9.6.3 (revised 2019, revised edition November 2024, corrections May 2025)
wording: Prior to discharge, follow up should be arranged with the patient’s general practitioner or asthma nurse within two working days and with a hospital specialist asthma nurse or respiratory physician at about one month after admission.

source: British Academy of Audiology, Guidance on Identifying Non-Routine Cases of Hearing Loss in Adults (April 2015)
wording: Sudden or rapid hearing loss: Either a greater than 30 dB deterioration in sensorineural hearing loss occurring in at least three adjacent audiometric frequencies over 72 hours or less, or rapid onset of hearing loss or rapid deterioration in hearing.

source: British Burn Association National Standards for burn care services (2023-24)
wording: Compliance: All burns over 20%TBSA have access to a single-bedded thermally controlled cubicle

source: British Society for Haematology, Guideline on the administration of blood components (2018, review ongoing)
wording: The Serious Hazards of Transfusion (SHOT) scheme has repeatedly identified that patients are harmed, and some die, as a result of being given the incorrect type of blood. SHOT therefore recommends a structured process with a bedside checklist.

source: British Society for Rheumatology shared care guidance for DMARD monitoring (as summarised by NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service)
wording: Risk factors for DMARD toxicity should be reviewed at least annually, adjusting the frequency of monitoring according to the level of risk identified. A shared care protocol should be agreed upon delineating the responsibilities of each party.

source: British Thoracic Society Guideline for oxygen use in adults in healthcare and emergency settings (2017, reviewed 2019-2024)
wording: For acutely ill patients not at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, a target saturation range of 94-98% is recommended; for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, a target range of 88-92% is recommended pending blood gas results.

source: British Thoracic Society guideline for oxygen use in adults in healthcare and emergency settings, summary of recommendations (2017), section 4
wording: Oxygen should be prescribed and a signature should be entered on the drug chart on each drug round.

source: Clexane pre-filled syringes, Summary of Product Characteristics section 4.2 (Sanofi, revised February 2022)
wording: Enoxaparin sodium can be administered SC either as a once daily injection of 150 IU/kg (1.5 mg/kg) or as twice daily injections of 100 IU/kg (1 mg/kg). The regimen should be selected by the physician based on an individual assessment including evaluation of the thromboembolic risk and of the risk of bleeding.

source: DAS, BAETS and ENT UK, Management of haematoma after thyroid surgery: consensus guidelines (Anaesthesia 2022)
wording: Thus, routine patient observations should be carried out at least hourly for first 6 h postoperatively ... Minimum monitoring includes wound inspection, early warning and pain scoring, as well as awareness for more subtle signs (agitation; anxiety; difficulty in breathing; discomfort).

source: Department of Health and Social Care, Care and support statutory guidance (Care Act 2014), paragraph 14.7
wording: Safeguarding means protecting an adult's right to live in safety, free from abuse and neglect. It is about people and organisations working together to prevent and stop both the risks and experience of abuse or neglect.

source: Drug misuse and dependence: UK guidelines on clinical management (2017), section 7.5.4.2
wording: The hospital doctor should ascertain, by independent means, the likely dose of methadone or buprenorphine to which the patient is tolerant, by confirming: the daily dose prescribed; when the last dose was dispensed; whether recently the medication has been collected regularly; the time the last dose was observed to be taken by supervised consumption.

source: FSRH Clinical Guideline: Emergency Contraception (March 2017, amended July 2023)
wording: All women requiring EC should be offered a Cu-IUD if appropriate as it is the most effective method of EC.

source: Faculty of Pain Medicine / RCoA 'Surgery and Opioids: Best Practice Guidelines 2021', Discharge Planning 3 and 4
wording: The hospital discharge letter should be available in a timely way and provided to all healthcare professionals involved in caring for the patient, including community pharmacists, to avoid an acute prescription of opioids inadvertently becoming a repeat prescription. The hospital discharge letter must explicitly state the recommended opioid dose, amount supplied and planned duration of use. ... Usually 5 days and no more than 7 days of opioids (including Tramadol) should be prescribed.

source: Fifth Consensus Guidelines for the Management of Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting: Executive Summary (Gan et al., Anesth Analg 2026;143:497–513), Guideline 3
wording: Guideline 3. Administer PONV prophylaxis using 2 interventions in adults at any risk for PONV ... Since most adult patients undergoing surgery and anesthesia will have at least one risk factor for PONV, a general multimodal approach is recommended for administering PONV prophylaxis.

source: Fifth Consensus Guidelines for the Management of Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting: Executive Summary (Gan et al., Anesth Analg 2026;143:497–513), Guideline 4
wording: Patients should receive rescue treatment from a different pharmacological class to the prophylactic agents administered. If more than 6 hours has elapsed, administration of a second dose of a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist or butyrophenone may be considered if no alternatives are available.

source: GIRFT National Suspected Cauda Equina Syndrome Pathway (February 2023, updated March 2026), Bladder scan
wording: If a patient is able to void, carefully document the following: • pre-void volume; • post-void residual volume (PVR)

source: GIRFT National Suspected Cauda Equina Syndrome Pathway (February 2023, updated March 2026), When to refer to the spinal surgical team
wording: Safety net about progression of CES symptoms via video and card

source: GIRFT touchtime utilisation target, as reported in PMC11488670 (CC BY)
wording: The Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT) programme has set targets to achieve 85% touchtime utilisation by 2024/25. Touchtime utilisation is a measure of theatre productivity, defined as the time from the start of anaesthesia to the time a patient leaves the theatre for all cases on a defined theatre list as a percentage of total available theatre time.

source: GOV.UK Supplying take home naloxone without a prescription (Human Medicines Regulations 2012, regulation 238; guidance updated 12 September 2025)
wording: The types of drug treatment services that can supply naloxone include, but may not be limited to: drug services provided by primary care services; drug services provided by secondary care services (including a range of specialised community and inpatient drug services)...

source: Gentamicin 40 mg/ml Solution for Injection or Infusion, Summary of Product Characteristics section 4.2 (Wockhardt UK, revised April 2024)
wording: Serum concentration monitoring of gentamicin is recommended, especially in elderly, in newborns and in patients with impaired renal function. Samples are taken at the end of a dosing interval (trough level). Trough levels should not exceed 2 µg/ml administering gentamicin twice daily and 1 µg/ml for a once daily dose.

source: Health Education England, Mouth Care Matters (2019), cited in a hospital Trust Mouthcare Policy CLP157
wording: It is suggested by (NHS Health Education Mouth Care Matters 2019) a mouth care assessment should be undertaken on admission or within 24 hours of admission and should be reviewed weekly.

source: Hospital Trust Mouthcare Policy CLP157, applying Health Education England's Mouth Care Matters standard
wording: Independent (Green), promote good oral mouth health care as a minimum of twice daily; Needs supervision/help to clean teeth (Amber)... Needs mouth care (Red), assist with mouth care.

source: Humphreys H et al., Surveillance of infection associated with external ventricular drains: proposed methodology and results from a multicentre study, Journal of Hospital Infection (Healthcare Infection Society), 2017
wording: The use of denominators that account for the duration of the device are preferable (e.g. per 1000 EVD-days) as the risk of infection increases the longer the EVD is in situ.

source: IR(ME)R 2017 regulation 12(3)(c) and UKHSA National Diagnostic Reference Levels (updated 11 December 2025), table 1 adult CT
wording: (3) Without prejudice to paragraphs (1) and (2), the operator must select equipment and methods to ensure that for each exposure the dose of ionising radiation to the individual undergoing the exposure is as low as reasonably practicable and consistent with the intended diagnostic or therapeutic purpose and in doing so must have regard, in particular to— ... (c) adherence to such diagnostic reference levels for radiodiagnostic examinations falling within regulation 3(a), (b), (e) and (f) as the employer may have established, as set out in the employer’s procedures. UKHSA table 1: Head, Acute stroke, All sequences, CTDIvol 47 mGy, DLP 790 mGy cm, adopted 2022.

source: Intercollegiate Green Theatre Checklist v2.0 (November 2024), item 12
wording: REPLACE: switch to low carbon alternatives (e.g. skin sutures vs. clips, "loose" antiseptic solutions in reusable gallipots).

source: Intercollegiate Green Theatre Checklist v2.0 (November 2024), item 14
wording: RECYCLE/use lowest carbon appropriate waste streams: use recycling waste streams for packaging or, if not available, domestic waste stream (prior to patient entering the room); use non-infectious offensive waste streams (yellow/black tiger) unless clear risk of infection (orange); ensure only appropriate contents in sharps bins (sharps/drugs)

source: Intercollegiate Green Theatre Checklist v2.0 (November 2024), item 3
wording: If using inhalational anaesthesia: use low-flow anaesthesia (via end-tidal anaesthetic gas control, if available).

source: Intercollegiate Green Theatre Checklist v2.0 (November 2024), item 6
wording: Evaluate PPE and sterile field requirements: rationalise use of non-sterile single-use gloves and PPE and opt for reusables when possible; limit sterile field to necessary areas only. Ensure availability of reusable textiles, including theatre hats, sterile gowns, patient drapes, and trolley covers.

source: Intercollegiate Green Theatre Checklist v2.0 (November 2024), item 8
wording: Avoid clinically unnecessary interventions (e.g. antibiotics, urinary catheterisation, histology examinations)

source: Intercollegiate Green Theatre Checklist v2.0 (November 2024), item 9
wording: REVIEW AND RATIONALISE: clarify necessary kit for case and specify what should be available to open only if needed: “Just in time”; take the opportunity to review instrument sets and identify any targets for overage reduction

source: Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017, Schedule 2 paragraph 1(j)
wording: The employer’s written procedures for exposures must include procedures— ... (j) for the carrying out and recording of a clinical evaluation for each exposure including, where appropriate, factors relevant to patient dose;

source: Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017, Schedule 2, paragraph 1(j)
wording: Schedule 2 sets out the data to be recorded for each exposure, including the radiation dose delivered, which for interventional procedures includes the dose-area product or equivalent dose metric for the procedure.

source: Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017, regulation 10(5)
wording: The referrer must supply the practitioner with sufficient medical data (such as previous diagnostic information or medical records) relevant to the exposure requested by the referrer to enable the practitioner to decide whether there is a sufficient net benefit as required by regulation 11(1)(b).

source: Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017, regulation 11(1)(f)
wording: A person must not carry out an exposure unless— ... (f) in the case of an individual of childbearing potential, the person has enquired whether that individual is pregnant or breastfeeding, if relevant.

source: Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017, regulation 11(1)(f); ARSAC Notes for Guidance on the Clinical Administration of Radiopharmaceuticals and Use of Sealed Radioactive Sources (January 2016), paragraph 7.3
wording: a person must not carry out an exposure unless... in the case of an individual of childbearing potential, the person has enquired whether that individual is pregnant or breastfeeding, if relevant. [IR(ME)R reg 11(1)(f)] Any female of childbearing potential undergoing procedures involving radiopharmaceuticals should therefore be asked whether she is or might be pregnant. A policy should be established on the age range of females involved (eg 12 to 55 years) and followed unless there are known exceptional circumstances applying to an individual patient. [ARSAC 7.3]

source: Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017, regulation 12 (Optimisation); ARSAC Notes for Guidance (January 2016), paragraph 3.11
wording: In some cases, if the patient is healthy and cooperative, activity might be reduced and scan times increased... it is important that the diagnostic information produced is not compromised by reduction in activity.

source: Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017, regulation 12(3)(c) (Optimisation); UKHSA National Diagnostic Reference Levels
wording: Regulation 12(3)(c) requires the employer to establish diagnostic reference levels for standard radiodiagnostic examinations and to ensure they are used as part of the optimisation of exposures; UKHSA publishes the National Diagnostic Reference Levels used to benchmark local practice.

source: Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017, regulation 17(4)
wording: The employer must keep and have available for inspection by the relevant enforcing authority an up-to-date record of all relevant training undertaken by all practitioners and operators engaged by the employer to carry out any exposures or any practical aspect of such exposures showing the date or dates on which training qualifying as adequate training was completed and the nature of the training.

source: Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017, regulations 10(2), 10(5) and 11(1)(b)
wording: A person must not carry out an exposure unless... it has been justified by the practitioner as showing a sufficient net benefit giving appropriate weight to the matters set out in paragraph (2) [reg 11(1)(b)]. The referrer must supply the practitioner with sufficient medical data... to enable the practitioner to decide whether there is a sufficient net benefit as required by regulation 11(1)(b) [reg 10(5)].

source: JBDS 01: The Hospital Management of Hypoglycaemia in Adults with Diabetes Mellitus (revised January 2023)
wording: Promote the prescription of hypoglycaemia “rescue” treatment for all people with diabetes in hospital on insulin or sulfonylurea therapy. This could involve a “PRN (pro re nata)” or “as needed” prescription of intravenous (IV) glucose and/or intramuscular (IM) glucagon.

source: JBDS 01: The Hospital Management of Hypoglycaemia in Adults with Diabetes Mellitus (revised January 2023), 'When hypoglycaemia has been successfully treated'
wording: Unless the cause is easily identifiable and both the nursing staff and the person with diabetes is confident steps can be taken to avoid future events, a medical or Diabetes Inpatient Specialist Nurse (DISN) review should be considered. If the hypoglycaemia event was severe or recurrent, or if the person voices concerns then a review is indicated

source: JBDS 02: The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults (revised March 2023)
wording: If the glucose falls below 14.0 mmol/L, commence 10% glucose given at 125 ml/hour alongside the 0.9% sodium chloride solution. In addition consider reducing the rate of intravenous insulin infusion to 0.05 units/kg/hr.

source: JBDS 02: The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults (revised March 2023), Best Practice Tariff standards table
wording: People admitted to hospital with diabetic ketoacidosis should be seen by member of the diabetes specialist team within 1 working day of admission

source: JBDS 06: The Management of the Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS) in Adults (February 2022)
wording: Everyone with HHS should receive prophylactic low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) for the full duration of admission unless contraindicated.

source: JBDS 06: The Management of the Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS) in Adults (February 2022), Insulin Dose and Timing
wording: if significant ketonaemia is not present do NOT start an intravenous insulin infusion

source: JBDS-IP 01 The Hospital Management of Hypoglycaemia in Adults with Diabetes Mellitus (revised January 2023), p11 step 4
wording: 4. Repeat capillary blood glucose measurement 10-15 minutes later. If it is still less than 4.0mmol/L, repeat step 3 (no more than 3 treatments in total). If it is above 4.0mmol/L then go to step 7.

source: JBDS-IP 02 The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults (revised March 2023), p15 and key recommendations
wording: In those already on long acting basal insulin, it should continue to be prescribed at their usual dose. In those newly diagnosed, then a long acting basal insulin should be commenced, at a dose of 0.25 units/Kg subcutaneously once daily. ... 4. Subcutaneous long-acting analogue/human insulin should be continued

source: JBDS-IP 08 Management of Hyperglycaemia and Steroid (Glucocorticoid) Therapy (revised January 2023), Table 1, p9
wording: Known diagnosis of diabetes: Reassess glucose control and current therapy. Set target blood glucose e.g. 6-10mmol/L. Check CBG 4 times a day and use this flowchart to adjust diabetes medication accordingly. In Type 1 diabetes also check daily for ketones if CBG >12mmol/L. Aim for 6-10mmol/L (acceptable range 6-12mmol/L).

source: JBDS-IP guideline JBDS 09: The use of variable rate intravenous insulin infusion (VRIII) in medical inpatients (current version, October 2014), Chapter 3 key message 2
wording: Continue patients' usual basal* subcutaneous insulin whilst on VRIII and stop rapid acting or mixed insulins

source: JBDS-IP guideline JBDS 09: The use of variable rate intravenous insulin infusion (VRIII) in medical inpatients (current version, October 2014), sections 3.7 and 3.7.1
wording: Avoid hypoglycaemia by providing substrate at a steady rate for the insulin infusion [...] Do not infuse insulin without substrate unless in HDU/ITU setting

source: Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, JBDS 01: The Hospital Management of Hypoglycaemia in Adults with Diabetes Mellitus (revised January 2023)
wording: If the person with diabetes in hospital has an insulin infusion in situ, stop immediately. Continue to follow the guidance below. Restart the insulin infusion once the hypo has been fully treated.

source: LSEBN, Burn Inhalation Injury protocol (2026)
wording: Review by senior anaesthetist and consider early intubation if there is a suspicion of BII: early intubation may decrease pulmonary-related mortality in patients with inhalation injury.

source: LSEBN, Facial Burns management (March 2026)
wording: Check eyes with fluorescein … Consider ophthalmology review if required

source: LSEBN, Initial management of ocular burns (2026, developed with Moorfields Eye Hospital)
wording: Check corneal ph (mean ph of tears is 7.6) … In chemical injuries, repeat the pH test soon after the irrigation has ceased and again 30 minutes later

source: LSEBN, Toxic Shock guideline (January 2026), section 2.3
wording: Provide TSS safety netting advice (verbal and written where possible)

source: Leicestershire Partnership NHS Trust Positive Patient Identification Policy (October 2023), based on the NHS identity band standard
wording: Patients in inpatient areas should wear identity bands, it is however recognised that patients with acute mental health needs or confusion may not agree to wearing an identity band. In these cases, and where there are documented efforts to explain to patients the purpose in relation to their safety, a patient photograph should be taken with the consent of the patient to provide an alternative means of identification.

source: Local standard
wording: Children and young people aged 8 to 16 years who present with hip, thigh or knee pain, or a limp, without a clear alternative cause, have an anteroposterior pelvis and frog-leg lateral X-rays of both hips before discharge from the Emergency Department.

source: Local standard (no national standard identified)
wording: Patients cancelled from a theatre list are offered food or drink within 60 minutes of the decision to cancel.

source: Local standard, based on NICE CG50 Acutely ill patients in hospital, rec 1.3 (2007) principle of physiological track-and-trigger monitoring for all acutely unwell patients regardless of location
wording: Physiological observations should be monitored at least every 12 hours, unless a decision has been made at a senior level to increase or decrease this frequency for an individual patient.

source: Local standard, based on the pain-severity thresholds used in RCEM's Pain in Children quality improvement programme (2021/22) extended to adults
wording: Patients in severe pain (pain score 7 or more out of 10) should receive their first dose of analgesia within 20 minutes of a pain score being recorded.

source: Local standard, informed by NICE guideline NG45 on routine preoperative tests for elective surgery and Choosing Wisely UK principles on avoiding unnecessary repeat testing
wording: Local standard: a repeat full blood count or urea and electrolytes test within 24 hours of a normal or unchanged previous result should have a documented new clinical indication (for example a change in condition, a new treatment started, or a scheduled monitoring protocol).

source: Local standard, informed by RCGP safeguarding recording principles and NHS England information-sharing requirements for safeguarding
wording: A safeguarding concern raised in a consultation should be recorded using a specific, searchable safeguarding code in the patient's electronic record, in addition to any free-text description, so that the concern can be identified for information sharing, multi-agency working and future risk assessment.

source: Local standard, informed by the NHS Constitution 18-week referral-to-treatment standard and British Academy of Audiology description of the routine adult hearing aid pathway
wording: Local standard: adults referred into the routine, direct-referral adult hearing aid pathway who are assessed as suitable for amplification should have their first hearing aid fitted within 18 weeks of referral, in line with the NHS referral-to-treatment standard, since (as the British Academy of Audiology notes) 'Routine, direct referral adult care pathways in the UK specifically fund hearing aid fitting'.

source: Local standard; 15-minute turnaround target as used in [2792]
wording: Turnaround (patient leaves theatre to start of the next patient's anaesthetic) of 15 minutes or less.

source: London and South East of England Burn Network (LSEBN), Initial management of burn wounds (2026)
wording: Cool with running tap water for 20 minutes within 3 hours of injury. If limited water supply, apply a cool compress, change frequently over 20-minute period. … Do not use ice/iced water/ice packs

source: MHRA Drug Safety Update volume 13 issue 3 (October 2019): Prescribing medicines in renal impairment
wording: creatinine clearance (CrCl) should be calculated using the Cockcroft-Gault formula (see below) to determine dosage adjustments for: direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs) [...] In particular, CrCl should always be used to guide dose adjustment for direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs; apixaban, dabigatran etexilate, edoxaban▼, and rivaroxaban▼). Use of eGFR for dosing of DOACs is known to increase risk of bleeding events as a consequence of overestimating renal function.

source: MHRA Drug Safety Update, 'Adrenaline auto-injectors: updated advice after European review' (August 2017)
wording: ensure that people with allergies and their carers have been trained to use the particular auto-injector that they have been prescribed—technique varies between injectors... You should review with the patient and their carers the instructions and operation of the adrenaline auto-injector.

source: MHRA Drug Safety Update, 'Isotretinoin: changes to prescribing guidance and additional risk minimisation measures' (22 January 2026)
wording: prescribers should monitor patients for side effects including mental health and sexual function side effects at each follow up appointment including objective mental health patient reported outcome measures

source: MHRA Drug Safety Update, 'Methotrexate once-weekly for autoimmune diseases: new measures to reduce risk of fatal overdose' (23 September 2020)
wording: decide with the patient which day of the week they will take their methotrexate and note this day down in full on the prescription

source: MHRA Drug Safety Update, 'Opioids: risk of dependence and addiction' (23 September 2020)
wording: before starting treatment with opioids, agree with the patient a treatment strategy and plan for end of treatment

source: MHRA Drug Safety Update, 'Valproate: dispense full packs of valproate-containing medicines' (31 October 2023)
wording: Unless there are exceptional circumstances, valproate-containing medicines must always be dispensed in the manufacturer's original full pack.

source: MHRA Drug Safety Update, April 2019 (valproate materials updated June 2025)
wording: It is the prescriber’s responsibility to ensure women and girls of childbearing potential (from menarche to menopause) who are taking a valproate medicine, irrespective of indication, fulfil all the requirements of the Pregnancy Prevention Programme. These responsibilities include that the patient (or responsible person) and their specialist must complete the Annual Risk Acknowledgement Form at each year’s annual review.

source: MHRA Drug Safety Update, August 2020: Denosumab 60mg (Prolia): increased risk of multiple vertebral fractures after stopping or delaying ongoing treatment (6-month-and-4-week window is a local standard)
wording: an increased risk of multiple vertebral fractures has been reported in patients within 18 months of stopping or delaying ongoing denosumab 60mg treatment for osteoporosis; cases have been reported in patients in the UK. patients should not stop denosumab without specialist review. if you miss a prescribed dose of denosumab, the missed injection should be administered as soon as possible. After this, your next injection will be scheduled 6 months from the date of your last injection

source: MHRA Drug Safety Update, February 2025: Valproate – review by two specialists is required for initiating valproate
wording: valproate must not be started in new patients (male or female) younger than 55 years unless two specialists independently consider and document that there is no other effective or tolerated treatment, or there are compelling reasons that the reproductive risks do not apply.

source: MHRA Drug Safety Update, January 2024 (valproate regulatory measures; materials updated June 2025)
wording: valproate must not be started in new patients (male or female) younger than 55 years, unless two specialists independently consider and document that there is no other effective or tolerated treatment, or there are compelling reasons that the reproductive risks do not apply ... at their next annual specialist review, women of childbearing potential and girls receiving valproate should be reviewed using the revised valproate Annual Risk Acknowledgement Form. A second specialist signature will be needed if the patient is to continue on valproate, however subsequent annual reviews will only require one specialist

source: MHRA Drug Safety Update, January 2024 (vol 17, issue 6: 2)
wording: the UK indications for systemic fluoroquinolones have been updated so they must only be used in situations when other antibiotics, that are commonly recommended for the infection, are inappropriate; situations in which other antibiotics are considered to be inappropriate and where a fluoroquinolone may be indicated are where: there is resistance to other first-line antibiotics recommended for the infection; other first-line antibiotics are contraindicated in an individual patient; other first-line antibiotics have caused side effects in the patient requiring treatment to be stopped; treatment with other first-line antibiotics has failed

source: MHRA Drug Safety Update, June 2024: Topiramate (Topamax): introduction of new safety measures, including a Pregnancy Prevention Programme
wording: topiramate should not be used in women of childbearing potential unless the conditions of the Pregnancy Prevention Programme are fulfilled. This aims to ensure that all women of childbearing potential: are using highly effective contraception; have a pregnancy test to exclude pregnancy before starting topiramate; are aware of the risks from use of topiramate

source: MHRA Drug Safety Update, March 2020: Benzodiazepines and opioids – reminder of risk of potentially fatal respiratory depression
wording: only prescribe benzodiazepines (or benzodiazepine-like drugs) and opioids together if there is no alternative; if a decision is made to co-prescribe, use the lowest doses possible for the shortest duration of time and carefully monitor patients for signs of respiratory depression

source: MHRA Drug Safety Update, October 2019: Prescribing medicines in renal impairment
wording: In particular, CrCl should always be used to guide dose adjustment for direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs; apixaban, dabigatran etexilate, edoxaban▼, and rivaroxaban▼). Use of eGFR for dosing of DOACs is known to increase risk of bleeding events as a consequence of overestimating renal function.

source: MHRA Drug Safety Update, October 2020
wording: Patients with complete or partial dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) deficiency are at increased risk of severe and fatal toxicity during treatment with these medicines. All patients should be tested for DPD deficiency before initiation to minimise the risk of these reactions.

source: MHRA Drug Safety Update, Oral retinoids: pregnancy prevention – reminder of measures to minimise teratogenic risk (2013, republished 2014; read with the 2023 and 2026 isotretinoin updates)
wording: Pregnancy must be excluded before treatment with oral retinoids … Pregnancy test results (with a minimum sensitivity of 25 mIU/mL) must be documented 3 days or less before the prescription is issued

source: MHRA Drug Safety Update, September 2012 (vol 6, issue 2: A1)
wording: where there is doubt over the timing of paracetamol ingestion including when ingestion has occurred over a period of one hour or more – 'staggered overdose' – acetylcysteine should be given without delay (the nomogram should not be used).

source: MHRA Drug Safety Update: Opioids: risk of dependence and addiction (23 September 2020)
wording: opioid medicines (opioids) provide relief from serious short-term pain; however long-term use in non-cancer pain (longer than 3 months) carries an increased risk of dependence and addiction [...] before starting treatment with opioids, agree with the patient a treatment strategy and plan for end of treatment

source: MHRA Drug Safety Update: haloperidol in elderly patients with delirium (10 December 2021)
wording: before initiating treatment, a baseline electrocardiogram (ECG) and correction of any electrolyte disturbances is recommended; cardiac and electrolyte monitoring should be repeated during treatment

source: MHRA Management and use of IVD point of care test devices (updated 14 July 2026), section 4.10 record keeping
wording: It is imperative to keep accurate records of patient results from POCT devices. These records should include: date; device type; batch numbers; result; operator identity; patient identity

source: MHRA Management and use of IVD point of care test devices (updated 14 July 2026), section 4.2 training
wording: Only staff whose training and competence has been established and recorded should be permitted to carry out POCT. They should also receive continued support and regular updates.

source: MHRA Safety guidelines for magnetic resonance imaging equipment in clinical use (version 5.0, July 2026), section 5.3.4 screening prior to examination, figure 5 stage 1
wording: Referrer completes targeted MRI screening questions as part of the MRI referral, designed to highlight any potential contraindications to MRI.

source: Manchester Triage Group / RCEM Triage position statement, summarised in RCEM Best Practice Guideline: Triage (2017, reviewed)
wording: Patients triaged as 'very urgent' (category 2) should be seen by a clinician within 10 minutes of arrival at triage.

source: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency, Bed rails: management and safe use (updated 2023)
wording: Chest or neck entrapment in bed rails is listed (number 11) as a 'Never Event' according to the NHS in 2018... Risk assessments should account for any characteristics which might put the bed user at greater risk from use of bed rails.

source: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (2015), paragraph 16.47
wording: Assessment by the doctor and AMHP should begin as soon as possible after the arrival of the individual at the place of safety. In cases where there are no clinical grounds to delay assessment, it is good practice for the doctor and AMHP to attend within three hours; this is in accordance with best practice recommendations made by the Royal College of Psychiatrists.

source: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (2015), paragraph 26.134
wording: Nursing reviews of the secluded patient should take place at least every two hours following the commencement of seclusion. These should be undertaken by two individuals who are registered nurses, and at least one of whom should not have been involved directly in the decision to seclude.

source: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (2015), paragraph 26.141
wording: An independent MDT review should be promptly undertaken where a patient has either been secluded for eight hours consecutively or for 12 hours intermittently during a 48-hour period.

source: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (2015), paragraph 26.147
wording: As a minimum the seclusion care plan should include: a statement of clinical needs (including any physical or mental health problems), risks and treatment objectives; a plan as to how needs are to be met, how de-escalation attempts will continue and how risks will be managed; details of bedding and clothing to be provided; details as to how the patient's dietary needs are to be provided for.

source: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (2015), paragraph 27.10
wording: When considering and planning leave of absence, responsible clinicians should: ... undertake a risk assessment and put in place any necessary safeguards ...

source: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (2015), paragraph 27.22
wording: Copies of the authorisation should be given to the patient and to any carers, professionals and other people in the community who need to know. A copy should also be kept in the patient's notes.

source: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (2015), paragraph 4.28
wording: Those with responsibility for patient care should ensure that patients are reminded from time to time of their rights and the effects of the Act. It may be necessary to give the same information on a number of different occasions or in different formats and to check regularly that the patient has fully understood it. Information given to a patient who is unwell may need to be repeated when their condition has improved.

source: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (2015), paragraph 6.16
wording: If a patient lacks capacity to decide whether or not to obtain help from an IMHA, the hospital manager should ask an IMHA to attend the patient so that the IMHA can explain what they can offer to the patient directly.

source: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (2015), paragraphs 26.144-26.145
wording: Seclusion should immediately end when a MDT review, a medical review or the independent MDT review determines it is no longer warranted... Seclusion ends when a patient is allowed free and unrestricted access to the normal ward environment or transfers or returns to conditions of long-term segregation.

source: NCEPOD, Risking Life and Limb: acute limb ischaemia national report
wording: In severe cases (Rutherford IIb), patients need to be treated by specialist staff within six hours of their symptoms appearing.

source: NCEPOD, Tracheostomy Care: On the Right Trach? (2014), recommendation 12
wording: Particularly careful consideration should be made at discharge from the critical care unit as to whether a cuffed tube is still indicated, and reasons must be documented. If it is, then there must be equipment and competences available on the ward for cuff pressure measurement.

source: NCEPOD, Tracheostomy Care: On the Right Trach? (2014), recommendation 14
wording: All hospitals should adhere to recommendations already made by the National Tracheostomy Safety Project to maintain an essential box of equipment which is sufficiently portable to be moved around with the patient.

source: NELA NoLap Standards of Care (from April 2024), end-of-life care, citing RCS Caring for Patients Nearing the End of Life
